items.quote: 3 But the more single and subtle part of the Galenists, who like Nicodemus are of a milder temper
items.what: the more single and subtle part of the Galenists
items.note: The paragraph opens with a printed 3 and sets apart one part of the Galenists, likened to Nicodemus; the earlier numbers of this run are not in the lines given.

items.quote: for fear of being excommunicated by some Athenian Rabbies, durst not openly professe the truth
items.note: This part of the Galenists is said to keep the truth unprofessed out of fear of persons called Athenian Rabbies; the lines given do not say who these are.

items.quote: these with open Arms will most readily imbrace this so long look't for, and desired light
items.note: Croll expects this milder part to welcome what he brings, which he calls a light long looked for.

items.quote: When envy and hatred give counsell, the Judgement is nothing worth.
items.note: The margin note beside the foreseen ill omen: a judgement counselled by envy and hatred is worthless.

items.quote: Envy which will certainly arise from hence, should grieve and be troubled that these things should be made common for publick use
items.note: Croll says these things are being made common for public use and foresees that envy will be troubled by exactly that.

items.quote: they will a little coldly commend those things, which notwithstanding are secretly reserved for their uses
items.note: The same men are foreseen to praise coldly in the open what they keep secretly for their own use.

items.quote: though (to such) without Gods blessing upon them
items.note: Croll holds that the things so reserved are without God's blessing for such users.

items.quote: But virtue can never be found without the marks and wounds of envy
items.note: Croll states that envy always accompanies virtue and those who work for the good of a Common-wealth.

items.quote: I study not to please all, for neither all men nor all things please me.
items.note: A first-person saying in the margin beside the passage on envy; the note does not show whether it is Croll's own sentence or one he cites.

items.quote: the hardest matter that can be, to doe an acceptable work to an ingratefull world
items.note: Croll calls the world ungrateful and his work hard to make acceptable to it; he adds that the envious deserve pity rather than envy.

items.quote: till in good time they willingly deliver themselves out of the Purgatory of their own malice
items.note: Purgatory is used as a figure: the text itself says it is the Purgatory of their own malice, which torments them.

items.quote: As for the more dull and drossie sort of them
items.what: the more dull and drossie sort of them
items.note: A further sort is set apart from the milder part of OPEN.12: those who reject the truth and take error for their Companion.

items.quote: these will angrily challenge and provoke this my good endeavour toward the publick, with most scornfull reproaches
items.note: Croll calls his work a good endeavour toward the publick and expects reproaches for it from this sort.

items.quote: according to the Comaedian, there can be nothing more unjust then these leud haters of Chymistry, and despisers of wisdome
items.name: the Comaedian
items.note: A judgement of injustice is given on the authority of one called the Comaedian, not named further in the lines given; Croll applies it to the haters of Chymistry.

items.quote: had rather dye in their old tract, and grosse folly, then be thought to learn of those whose Masters they accounted themselves to be
items.note: Croll says these men would rather die in their old way than be seen to learn from those they counted their pupils.

items.quote: There is a two-fold Alchymy. Naturall, much esteemed by Artist. Sophisticall, as much detested by them.
items.note: The margin note divides Alchymy into two, Naturall and Sophisticall, the one esteemed and the other detested by those it calls Artist.

items.quote: these insolent and open contemners of Natures secrets, who tremble at the very name of Chymistry
items.note: Nature is said to have secrets, which the opponents despise; Chymistry is named in the same breath.

items.quote: shamelesly to scoff at this Divine Art
items.note: Croll calls Chymistry this Divine Art.

items.quote: whereas they never yet so much as saluted it at the threshold
items.note: Croll says the revilers abuse an art they have never so much as approached.

items.quote: trample upon the Truth, and those Pearls cast before them
items.note: Pearls is a figure. Interpreted (my inference): the Pearls are what is offered to these men together with the Truth, since both are trampled in the one phrase; the lines given do not say more.

items.quote: their Captain, that railing Binarius
items.note: The opponents are given a Captain under the name Binarius, who supplies their weapons; the lines given do not say who or what is meant by the name.

items.quote: there is no other reason why it should be sent to the Isle Anticyra
items.note: Their rage and Cyclopean fury is to be sent to a place named the Isle Anticyra; the lines given do not explain the place, so the phrase points beyond its plain sense without stating it.

items.quote: (as they themselves will privately and openly confesse) their ignorance of the just and due preparation of things
items.name: they themselves
items.note: Croll gives as the one reason of their fury their ignorance of the preparation of things, and says the opponents themselves will confess it.

items.quote: to determine of those as if we were well acquainted with them, is not only foolish, but filthy
items.note: Croll holds that to pass judgement on unknown things as if known is foolish and filthy.

items.quote: such Scholastick Doctors, who for want of wit could never find the way into Natures Sanctuary
items.note: Nature is given a Sanctuary into which the Scholastick Doctors never found the way.

items.quote: doe no lesse then the common people, admire, as Magical Miracles, those eminent works wherein the whole power of Nature flourisheth
items.note: Croll says the Doctors, once convinced, wonder like the common people at works he ascribes to the power of Nature; Magical Miracles is how they are admired, not his own name for them.

items.quote: many famous Phisitians of our time, equall to the most learned of men, who have spent all their life in the works of Art, men skill'd in the secrets of Nature
items.note: Croll sets against the Doctors a group of physicians of his time whom he praises as skilled in the secrets of Nature and spent in the works of Art.

items.quote: John 5.44.
items.name: John
items.note: A margin note naming a writing by chapter and verse, set where the text turns to the Honours of the world these physicians have not taken.

items.quote: they have not taken upon them those most vain Honours of the world
items.note: Croll calls the academic honours most vain; these physicians are condemned for not having taken them.

items.quote: See Paracels. Tom. 5. in fragm. Medicis. fol. 167, 168.
items.name: Paracels.
items.note: The margin note sends the reader to a named place in a writing of Paracels. beside the passage on honours and titles.

items.quote: It is a wicked Tyranny to captivate the fancy of Students to certain Authors, and take away the freedome of finding out and following the truth from young Scholars.
items.note: The note condemns binding students to certain authors; it follows the reference to Paracels. and does not show whether the sentence is his or Croll's.

items.quote: Money and Friends advance more then desert.
items.note: The note says advancement goes by money and friends more than by desert.

items.quote: (as they call them) the Authorities and Titles of Doctorship
items.name: they
items.note: The names Authorities and Titles of Doctorship are given as the opponents' own words for the honours; a gap of one illegible letter follows the last word.

items.quote: with which neither Hippocrates nor Galen, nor any Phisitians that we read of in their time were indowed or adorned
items.note: Croll argues that Hippocrates and Galen, authentic in the opponents' own opinion, bore no such titles.

items.quote: least they should be made to swear to the Heathenish errors of the School-Gods, against the naked Truth, and be bound by an Academicall Oath, to live and dye in them
items.note: The reason given why these physicians refuse the titles: the oath would bind them to what Croll calls the Heathenish errors of the School-Gods.

items.quote: these personated Titles heretofore by a commendable institution were the spur of virtue, and the deserved reward of Learning
items.note: Croll grants that the titles were once a commendable institution and a deserved reward.

items.quote: now adayes, especially in Phisick, they are bestowed either through flattery or bribery
items.note: Croll says the titles are now given, in Phisick above all, by flattery or bribery.

items.quote: The Earth hideth the error of such Physitians
items.note: The note says the errors of such physicians are hidden by the Earth; the same note speaks of their enriching the Church-yard.

items.quote: as Socrates saith of rash Physitians, sport & play with mans skin, or rather the Image of God
items.name: Socrates
items.note: A saying about rash physicians playing with man's skin is given to Socrates; the words or rather the Image of God stand as an added correction, and the note does not show whose they are.

items.quote: I speak not of those who obtain the true Titles and Bayes of their, Degrees by their deserts in Learning
items.note: Croll exempts from his charge those who earn their degrees by learning.

items.quote: they have found the brittlenesse by the losse of so noble a vessel
items.note: Vessel is not said plainly. Interpreted (my inference): the noble vessel lost is the patient, since the same sentence goes on to whether the Patient live or die and N026 speaks of man's skin and the Image of God.

items.quote: proceeding according to their method whereby they excuse all their errors, whether the Patient live or die
items.note: Croll says the titled physicians' method serves to excuse their errors whatever the outcome.

items.quote: whether Galens Axioms (as he writeth) doe any more concern us, then they doe wild Bears and Bores
items.name: he
items.note: The comparison with wild Bears and Bores is given as something a writer has written (as he writeth); the lines given do not show whether he is Galen or another.

items.quote: whether his Method of Phisick, wherein this Age so much triumpheth, hath any good foundation, being not supported with any Authority of Antiquity
items.note: Croll says they question, and not without cause, whether Galen's Method of Phisick has a foundation, and states that it lacks the authority of antiquity.

items.quote: they are Ocularly convinced that the end doth not answer his beginning in the great Cures of Diseases
items.note: The ground given for the doubt is what they see with their own eyes: in great cures the outcome does not match the method's promise.

items.quote: the Art of Phisick is so immense and large, that we may well account it as a very great blessing if (which is sufficient) we attain unto it even in the beginning of our old Age
items.note: Croll holds the Art of Phisick so large that to reach it by the start of old age is a blessing and enough.

items.quote: they plead in defence of their sloth and idlenesse, that they need not take any more paines for further knowledge, having the benefit of other mens labours and observations
items.name: they
items.note: The opponents' plea, reported by Croll in order to reject it: other men's labours and observations spare them further pains.

items.quote: God onely is Lord and Master of Nature
items.note: The note beside the passage on arrogance: God alone is Master of Nature.

items.quote: although it may give greater authority in the world, and vaine glorious estimation of a Name
items.note: The note says a Degree or Title gives worldly authority and the estimation of a name; the words before, on its not making wiser or more learned, hold a gap of two illegible letters.

items.quote: they ought to become Schollars and servants, not Doctors and Masters of Nature
items.note: Croll says the physician's place toward Nature is that of scholar and servant, and that these men will have to begin anew.

items.quote: How many of this sort of Phisitians have come with their gray haires complaining unto me?
items.note: Croll speaks of his own experience: old physicians of this sort came to him with complaints.

items.quote: Fooleries are to be forgotten.
items.note: The note beside the old physicians' complaint; a gap marked as foreign script follows it.

items.quote: in the common toyes of School-vanities, and in Phisicall notions, nothing at all availing to the effecting of their cures
items.note: Croll says the school learning in which they spent their time did nothing for their cures.

items.quote: like those that feed on Crabs and Crevises, they find much shell but little meat
items.note: A comparison the text applies itself (Stated): the school studies are like shellfish, much shell and little meat.

items.quote: having first cast away Opinion and Scorne the lets of learning
items.note: Croll names Opinion and Scorne as the hindrances of learning, cast away before these men came to knowledge of their errors.

items.quote: The world is ruled by Opinion.
items.note: The note beside the casting away of Opinion.

items.quote: to put off their old skin, like the wise Serpent, and putting on a new one, to become Schollars of Chymistry
items.note: The change of skin is a figure whose sense the text gives in the same clause (Stated): in old age they became Schollars of Chymistry.

items.quote: spend the rest of their dayes with those Secrets which are both in God and Nature
items.note: Secrets are said to lie both in God and in Nature; the study of Chymistry is set beside them.

items.quote: God is the first book that teacheth us eternall life: for the rule of life is from God.
items.note: The note names God as the first book and says what it teaches: eternall life.

items.quote: it is a lovely thing for old men to study Wisdome
items.note: Croll approves of old men studying Wisdome.

items.quote: with Diogenes, not give over the Race that they are running
items.name: Diogenes
items.note: Not giving over the race is linked to Diogenes by name; the lines given say no more of him.

items.quote: The firmament or heaven with all therein is the second Naturall book conducing to a mortall life
items.note: The note says what the second book is: the firmament or heaven with all in it, serving mortal life.

items.quote: for the knowledge of Phisick is got from the Stars
items.note: The note gives as its reason that the knowledge of Phisick comes from the Stars.

items.quote: next after the great book of Grace, wherein the eternall health of our soules consisteth
items.note: The text names a book of Grace, placed first, in which the eternal health of souls consists.

items.quote: that other also of Nature, treating of those Secrets which respect our bodily health
items.note: A second book, of Nature, is named; it treats of the Secrets that concern bodily health.

items.quote: those choise treasures of Nature, wherein the most High hath laid up medicines for our greatest and worst diseases
items.note: Medicines are said to be laid up by the most High in treasures of Nature, which are not to be passed by unnoticed.

items.quote: God is the first book
items.note: The note names God as the first book, the paragraph names the first book the great book of Grace; likewise N031 names the second the firmament or heaven, the paragraph the book of Nature. The lines given do not say that the two namings are one.

items.quote: buried in the dead shadows of meer outsides
items.note: Dead shadows of meer outsides is a figure for what these physicians do not want to die in; the words that follow set it beside the externall Galenicall qualities.

items.quote: The happines of this present life consisteth in the knowledge of Nature
items.note: The note places the happiness of this life in the knowledge of Nature.

items.quote: in temporalls the chiefest thing is to find out the secrets of Nature
items.note: The note says Nature has secrets and ranks finding them out first among temporal things, next after eternal ones.

items.quote: or the externall Galenicall qualities
items.note: The or joins this phrase to meer outsides just before the note mark: the outsides are named as the external qualities of the Galenicall teaching.

items.quote: they have built a stately Structure and a Temple as a most honourable monument to their old age and Nature
items.note: A building is spoken of that the lines do not describe as stone. Interpreted (my inference): it stands for what these old physicians gained as Schollars of Chymistry (OPEN.17), since Out of which they are said to obtain knowledge and the fruit of their labours.

items.quote: unto which they have attained as well by the sedulous search and admiration of the works of God
items.note: Croll says the clearer knowledge of the Creator is reached by searching and admiring the works of God.

items.quote: by their laborious examination, and Phylosophicall sequestration of the Creatures, or Naturall things
items.note: Work done on the Creatures, glossed as Naturall things, is named: examination and Phylosophicall sequestration. The lines given name the work but describe no step of it.

items.quote: this excellent fruit of their labours, watchings, time and experiences
items.what: this excellent fruit of their labours, watchings, time and experiences
items.note: A result is announced as one thing, next to the knowledge of the Creator; the viz. that follows says what it is.

items.quote: One shall not repent of such a Phisitian who hath the true knowledg of earthly things.
items.note: The note commends the physician who has true knowledge of earthly things.

items.quote: Vid: Agrip: lib. 6. Epist. c.
items.name: Agrip:
items.note: The note sends the reader to a named place in a writing of Agrip: beside the fruit of the labours.

items.quote: That when they shall be sent for to the sick (where not many words to dispute, but much skill to cure availeth most) they may come as well experienced Phisitians
items.note: The fruit is stated: they come to the sick as experienced physicians; Croll adds that with the sick skill to cure counts, not disputing.

items.quote: not pretending now to study that disease which they intend to patch up with some outward flattering plaister
items.note: Croll sets the experienced physician against one who only patches a disease outwardly while pretending to study it.

items.quote: with a multitude of frivolous services, and sugured words to cloak their simplicity
items.note: The covering here is the common physicians' own: services and sweet words cloak their lack of skill.

items.quote: the end of Phisick is not to scrape up money, but to discover the secrets of Nature, and the love of the Phisitian to the sick
items.note: The note says what the end of Phisick is and is not; its opening words hold two gaps of one illegible word each.

items.quote: insinuating into the richer sort for base gaine, but altogether slighting others of meaner fortune
items.note: Croll charges the common sort of proud physicians with courting the rich for gain and slighting the poor.

items.quote: every where forbid, as poisonous, those Phisicall Secrets
items.name: this ribble rabble
items.note: The judgement poisonous is the opponents', reported by Croll in order to reject it; he himself calls the things Phisicall Secrets.

items.quote: inventions of (Chymists, which they call) Collier-like-Phisitians
items.name: they
items.note: Collier-like-Phisitians is given as the opponents' name for the Chymists.

items.quote: they have a secret and subtle desire to learne those things which they hope to use with success and profit
items.note: The men who forbid these things in public are said to desire in secret to learn and use them.

items.quote: robbing the Inventers of the Art, and their Benefactours, of their deserved honour by a mendacious and inverted theft
items.note: Croll charges them with taking the praise due to the true author of medicines they got by craft.

items.quote: To these A pule jan Bravadoes, whether they put on the Lyons or the Foxes skin
items.note: The men just described are given a name, printed A pule jan Bravadoes, and two skins, the Lyons and the Foxes; the lines given do not explain the name.

items.quote: admission to the Bath of Diana is not to be granted
items.note: Something called the Bath of Diana is to be kept closed to these men; the lines given do not say what the Bath of Diana is.

items.quote: because Pythagoras forbids to put our victualls into a close stool
items.name: Pythagoras
items.note: A prohibition given to Pythagoras is the reason stated for refusing admission; victualls and close stool are applied by the text to what is offered and to those unworthy of it.

items.quote: nor should we bestow our choicest herbs on such as rudely rush into the Chymists garden, seeing brambles and thistles will serve their turne
items.note: The choicest herbs of a Chymists garden are to be withheld from those who rush in rudely; garden and herbs are not explained in the lines given.

items.quote: the calumnies and reproaches of leud and ignorant men are, in the opinion of the wise, not to be regarded by heroike spirits
items.name: the wise
items.note: That reproaches of the ignorant are to be disregarded is given as the opinion of the wise.

items.quote: The boyling pot doth {G014: 1 letter illegible}ot {G015: 1 letter illegible}ear the siege of flies.
items.note: The note repeats, in other words and with two one-letter gaps, the saying of the pot and the flies that stands in the paragraph.

items.quote: the flye never falls into the seething pot
items.note: A saying set beside the disregard of calumnies. Interpreted (my inference): the seething pot stands for the heroike spirits and the flye for the revilers, since the saying follows directly on them.

items.quote: the more humane and civill inclinations also of some make me expect better things
items.note: Croll expects better of some, once hatred of Truth and violent censures are laid aside.

items.quote: wherewith some have endeavoured to make such gifts of God suspected and hated by poor and rich
items.note: Croll calls the things censured gifts of God.

items.quote: would I for the unworthinesse of some shut these doors against those that seek after the true and Ancient Phisick
items.note: Croll speaks of doors he will not shut on seekers of the true and Ancient Phisick because of the unworthy; the word before the quote is damaged by a one-letter gap, and the clause runs beside I would not that good men earlier in the sentence.

items.quote: give place to Paracelsus according to his desert in practice and preparations
items.note: Croll asks that Paracelsus be given his due place in practice and preparations.

items.quote: admission to the Bath of Diana is not to be granted, because Pythagoras forbids to put our victualls into a close stool
items.note: Here admission and the choicest herbs are refused to some, while OPEN.12 speaks of these things being made common for publick use; the same paragraph goes on to say the doors are not shut on true seekers.

items.quote: these things here mentioned in this place, and in these times, may not be at all judged superfluous or beside the matter in hand
items.note: Croll defends his accusations as fitting the place and the times.

items.quote: neither will this Discourse offend any holy and Learned Phisitian
items.note: Croll says no holy and learned physician is touched by his Discourse.

items.quote: which I intend onely against those proud, envious, ignorant vassalls, who oppose the Chymicall verity against conscience
items.note: Croll limits his attack to those who oppose what he calls the Chymicall verity against their conscience.

items.quote: But before I come to describe the Remedies
items.note: Croll points forward to a description of the Remedies that is to come after what he handles first; that description is not in the lines given.

items.quote: I handle some things in this Admonitary Preface
items.note: Croll names the present writing, here spelled Admonitary, and announces the things it handles; the numbered heads follow.

items.quote: which with greatest intention of mind, and most diligent scruting, are to be explained by a Philosophicall Phisitian
items.note: Croll holds that these matters are for a Philosophicall Phisitian to explain, with the greatest attention.

items.quote: What that Phisick is which cureth mens diseases, and few Phisitians know it.
items.what: What that Phisick is which cureth mens diseases
items.note: The head numbered I of the things the Preface handles.

items.quote: and few Phisitians know it
items.note: The Phisick that cures is said to be known to few physicians.

items.quote: Whereunto is added a perfect Philosophicall Description of the little World Man, almost forgotten and unknown.
items.what: a perfect Philosophicall Description of the little World Man
items.note: A second matter is announced under the same number I, as an addition.

items.quote: the little World Man
items.note: The words set little World and Man side by side as names of one thing.

items.quote: almost forgotten and unknown
items.note: Several defensible readings: the words may say that the Description is almost forgotten and unknown, or that the little World Man is; the sentence allows both.

items.quote: Where that True Phisick lyeth hid, and may be found.
items.what: Where that True Phisick lyeth hid, and may be found
items.note: The head numbered II.

items.quote: that True Phisick lyeth hid
items.note: The True Phisick is said to lie hid in a place, and to be findable there.

items.quote: That it is to be fetcht out, and prepared truly, by fire.
items.what: That it is to be fetcht out, and prepared truly, by fire
items.note: The head numbered III.

items.quote: fetcht out, and prepared truly, by fire
items.note: Two things are done to the Phisick, both by fire: it is fetched out of where it lies and it is prepared; no further step is given in these lines.

items.quote: With what vertue, and after what manner, that Phisick worketh on mans body, and expelleth his diseases.
items.what: With what vertue, and after what manner, that Phisick worketh on mans body
items.note: The head numbered IV.

items.quote: What manner of Phisitian that Phisick doth require for its Minister.
items.what: What manner of Phisitian that Phisick doth require for its Minister
items.note: The head numbered V; the physician is called the Minister of the Phisick.

items.quote: Of the universall and chiefe Medicine or Phisick of the most Ancient Philosophers
items.what: the universall and chiefe Medicine or Phisick of the most Ancient Philosophers
items.note: The head numbered VI names one Medicine as universal and chief and gives it to the most Ancient Philosophers.

items.quote: commended of many, possessed, yea seen, or believed of very few
items.note: This Medicine is said to be praised by many but possessed, seen or even believed by very few.

items.quote: Some thing in defence of the published Truth, as an Epilogue or Conclusion.
items.note: A last, unnumbered head is announced: a defence of the Truth, which is called published.
